editorial_note: Readings of the registered claims, with concrete examples and source references. The families provide a reading order; proof evidence is reported separately.

claims.title: Find the entry that belongs to a key
claims.scenario: The list contains key 11 for 100¢ and key 22 for 50¢. Look up key 22.
claims.must_happen: Ledger.find and the independently written Spec.lookup must return the same answer, including when a key is absent.
claims.wrong_behavior: Return key 11’s entry when the lookup asks for key 22, or report a stored key as missing.
claims.why_others_miss: The list can be well formed and its totals correct while a lookup picks the wrong entry.
claims.does_not_cover: The input list must be proper and have unique keys. The lookup query itself is not restricted to integers.
claims.risk: Return key 11’s entry when the lookup asks for key 22, or report a stored key as missing.

claims.title: Change a status without changing who holds what
claims.scenario: Key 11 holds 100¢ and key 22 holds 50¢. Change key 11 from reserved to sent.
claims.must_happen: Every existing key and its original amount must remain in the entry list after the status replacement.
claims.wrong_behavior: Change key 11’s amount to 50¢, or drop key 22 while replacing key 11’s status.
claims.why_others_miss: A list can still contain unique, well-formed entries after an amount has been overwritten.
claims.does_not_cover: This helper claim preserves keys and amounts. It does not decide which status a payment event should choose.
claims.risk: Change key 11’s amount to 50¢, or drop key 22 while replacing key 11’s status.

claims.title: Count exactly what one status change adds or removes
claims.scenario: Key 11 is sent for 100¢. Replace its status with declined.
claims.must_happen: The holding total must fall by 100¢ and the holding count by one. A change between two holding statuses must leave both totals unchanged.
claims.wrong_behavior: Stop counting the 100¢ but leave its slot occupied when the entry becomes declined.
claims.why_others_miss: Keeping the key, amount and list shape says nothing about the sum and count calculated from the statuses.
claims.does_not_cover: These are totals calculated from the entry list. Updating a state’s stored counters is checked by the state-validity claims.
claims.risk: Stop counting the 100¢ but leave its slot occupied when the entry becomes declined.

claims.title: Keep the entry list well formed when a status changes
claims.scenario: A proper list has one 100¢ entry for key 11. Replace its reserved status with sent.
claims.must_happen: The result must still be a proper list of valid entries with unique keys.
claims.wrong_behavior: Append a second copy of key 11 instead of replacing its status in the existing entry.
claims.why_others_miss: The original key and amount would still be present, so identity preservation alone would miss the duplicate.
claims.does_not_cover: The replacement status must be known and the key must already exist. Account limits and cached counters are outside this helper claim.
claims.risk: Append a second copy of key 11 instead of replacing its status in the existing entry.

claims.title: Count a fresh reserved entry once
claims.scenario: A well-formed list has no key 11. Add key 11 as a reserved hold for 100¢.
claims.must_happen: The new list must keep unique keys and valid entries, add 100¢ to the holding total, and add one holding entry.
claims.wrong_behavior: Add the reserved entry but omit its 100¢ from the calculated holding total.
claims.why_others_miss: Lookup and status-replacement claims do not describe what happens when a fresh entry is added.
claims.does_not_cover: This is a claim about constructing an entry list. PO-A2 separately checks whether a fresh request fits the account’s limits.
claims.risk: Add the reserved entry but omit its 100¢ from the calculated holding total.

claims.title: Keep the same holding totals when sends become unknown
claims.scenario: The list contains a sent hold for 100¢ and an authorized hold for 50¢. Mark in-flight sends unknown.
claims.must_happen: The list must still account for 150¢ and two holding entries after Ledger.mark_unknown runs.
claims.wrong_behavior: Treat the newly unknown 100¢ entry as free when calculating the post-restart holding total.
claims.why_others_miss: Both sent and unknown are well-formed statuses; checking list structure alone would not catch a changed total.
claims.does_not_cover: This claim checks calculated totals. PO-B7 also checks that restart leaves no sent entries and preserves the stored counters.
claims.risk: Treat the newly unknown 100¢ entry as free when calculating the post-restart holding total.

claims.title: Start with a valid account state
claims.scenario: Initialize an account with an amount limit of 100¢ and one hold slot. Also consider limits of zero.
claims.must_happen: Every pair of nonnegative integer limits must produce a state whose entries, counters and limits satisfy Spec.valid?.
claims.wrong_behavior: Initialize the account with 100¢ marked used even though there are no holding entries.
claims.why_others_miss: Step-preservation claims start by assuming a valid state. They do not establish that initialization provides one.
claims.does_not_cover: The written conclusion checks validity. The separate policy describes the exact empty starting state and rejection of invalid arguments.
claims.risk: Initialize the account with 100¢ marked used even though there are no holding entries.

claims.title: Keep request handling within the account limits
claims.scenario: An account already holds its full 100¢. A fresh key requests another 50¢.
claims.must_happen: The request’s next state must have matching entries and counters, with used amount and hold count within their limits.
claims.wrong_behavior: Admit the extra 50¢ and leave the account using 150¢ against its 100¢ limit.
claims.why_others_miss: PO-A2 requires admission for requests that fit. This claim also covers over-capacity requests and malformed key or amount arguments.
claims.does_not_cover: A valid result can still be the wrong policy result. In particular, refusing every request would satisfy validity alone.
claims.risk: Admit the extra 50¢ and leave the account using 150¢ against its 100¢ limit.

claims.title: Admit a request that fits exactly
claims.scenario: An empty account has a 100¢ limit and one free slot. Fresh key 11 requests 100¢.
claims.must_happen: Return admitted, add key 11 as reserved, increase the used amount by 100¢ and the hold count by one, and request no outside work.
claims.wrong_behavior: Return insufficient_amount because the admission check rejects an exact fit. M4 makes this mistake; M5 refuses every eligible request.
claims.why_others_miss: Refusing the request leaves an empty, valid state. A validity check alone does not require the service to admit an eligible request.
claims.does_not_cover: The promise applies when request_eligible? holds: a valid account, fresh integer key, positive integer amount, free slot and sufficient amount capacity.
claims.risk: Return insufficient_amount because the admission check rejects an exact fit. M4 makes this mistake; M5 refuses every eligible request.

claims.title: Leave the account alone when an event is not applied
claims.scenario: An account holds 100¢ under key 11. A dispatch for absent key 22 returns not_found.
claims.must_happen: A non-applied result must return the entire original state and an empty requested-effects list.
claims.wrong_behavior: Return not_found for key 22 while changing key 11 or requesting an authorization anyway.
claims.why_others_miss: Those changes could leave a valid state. This claim requires exact state equality and no outside work.
claims.does_not_cover: The condition uses the result returned by the code. Other claims and the policy decide whether that result was the right one.
claims.risk: Return not_found for key 22 while changing key 11 or requesting an authorization anyway.

claims.title: Recognize a request even after its hold ends
claims.scenario: Key 11 is remembered as voided for 300¢. The same key requests 300¢ again.
claims.must_happen: Return duplicate with the entire state unchanged and no requested effects, regardless of the remembered status.
claims.wrong_behavior: Create another hold under the voided key and reserve its 300¢ again, as M1 attempts.
claims.why_others_miss: A capacity check can find enough free space after release. It does not establish whether this identity has already been used.
claims.does_not_cover: The new request uses an integer key and the original positive integer amount. A different positive amount belongs to the conflict claim.
claims.risk: Create another hold under the voided key and reserve its 300¢ again, as M1 attempts.

claims.title: Reject a reused key with a different amount
claims.scenario: Key 11 already records a 100¢ hold. Another request uses key 11 for 50¢, even though the account is full.
claims.must_happen: Return conflict, preserve the entire state and request no outside work. The identity check comes before the capacity checks.
claims.wrong_behavior: Overwrite key 11’s 100¢ with 50¢, or report insufficient_amount instead of the required conflict.
claims.why_others_miss: Both refusal results could leave the state valid. This claim checks the exact result and the unchanged state.
claims.does_not_cover: The incoming amount must be a different positive integer. Malformed requests are handled by the event policy.
claims.risk: Overwrite key 11’s 100¢ with 50¢, or report insufficient_amount instead of the required conflict.

claims.title: Keep the totals correct when a hold is dispatched
claims.scenario: Key 11 is reserved for 100¢, with 100¢ and one slot already counted. Dispatch it.
claims.must_happen: The next state must remain valid: the entries and stored totals agree and both limits are respected.
claims.wrong_behavior: Count the 100¢ a second time when its status changes from reserved to sent.
claims.why_others_miss: An authorization request can name the right key and amount even when the stored counters are wrong.
claims.does_not_cover: Validity does not require the precise sent transition or its authorization request. Read the effects claim and event policy for those details.
claims.risk: Count the 100¢ a second time when its status changes from reserved to sent.

claims.title: Keep an unknown hold in the totals
claims.scenario: Key 11 is sent for 300¢. Its authorization reply times out.
claims.must_happen: The next state must still have counters that match its holding entries and respect both limits.
claims.wrong_behavior: Keep key 11 as unknown but subtract its 300¢ and one slot from the counters. This is M2’s fault.
claims.why_others_miss: PO-B2 can preserve an unknown entry’s key and amount without checking the stored counters. This validity claim checks their agreement.
claims.does_not_cover: Changing the entry to declined and releasing it can be internally valid. The retention claim is needed to reject that invented terminal result.
claims.risk: Keep key 11 as unknown but subtract its 300¢ and one slot from the counters. This is M2’s fault.

claims.title: Keep restart’s entries and counters in agreement
claims.scenario: An account holds 100¢ as sent and 50¢ as authorized. Apply restart.
claims.must_happen: The resulting state must have correct amount and hold counters within the configured limits.
claims.wrong_behavior: Leave both holding entries in place but reset the used counters to zero on restart.
claims.why_others_miss: Removing every sent label would not catch counters that no longer match the remaining unknown and authorized entries.
claims.does_not_cover: Leaving a sent entry unchanged can still satisfy validity. PO-B7 checks that restart actually removes sent statuses.
claims.risk: Leave both holding entries in place but reset the used counters to zero on restart.

claims.title: Keep retry from counting the hold twice
claims.scenario: Key 11 is unknown for 100¢, already using one slot. Retry the authorization.
claims.must_happen: The retry’s next state must preserve the relationship between holding entries, used counters and account limits.
claims.wrong_behavior: Add another 100¢ and another slot to the counters even though the same entry is being retried.
claims.why_others_miss: Reusing the correct key in the authorization request does not by itself check the account’s stored totals.
claims.does_not_cover: A valid next state can accompany an incorrect requested effect. PO-B3 checks that retry requests the original identity and amount.
claims.risk: Add another 100¢ and another slot to the counters even though the same entry is being retried.

claims.title: Keep processor results from corrupting the totals
claims.scenario: Key 11 is sent for 300¢. The processor returns declined.
claims.must_happen: Handling the result must leave a valid state, with used counters matching the remaining holding entries.
claims.wrong_behavior: Increase used amount when the 300¢ hold is declined, as M8 does.
claims.why_others_miss: A declined entry can keep its correct key and amount while the cached amount total moves in the wrong direction.
claims.does_not_cover: Validity alone does not choose between approved and declined behavior. The event policy and independent reference specify the full result.
claims.risk: Increase used amount when the 300¢ hold is declined, as M8 does.

claims.title: Keep cancellation accounting internally consistent
claims.scenario: Key 11 is authorized for 100¢. A cancellation request arrives.
claims.must_happen: The returned state must have well-formed entries, correct holding totals and counters within the limits.
claims.wrong_behavior: Mark key 11 voiding while reporting that its 100¢ and one slot are free.
claims.why_others_miss: Remembering the key and requesting the right remote void do not ensure that the stored totals still count the hold.
claims.does_not_cover: A voided entry with zero used counters is also valid. This claim alone therefore permits P01’s premature release; retention supplies the missing requirement.
claims.risk: Mark key 11 voiding while reporting that its 100¢ and one slot are free.

claims.title: Keep an unresolved hold’s identity and amount
claims.scenario: Key 11 is unknown for 100¢. Retry it, or process an event that does not settle that key’s authorization.
claims.must_happen: Key 11 must remain unknown or sent with its original 100¢, and all previously recorded keys and amounts must remain present.
claims.wrong_behavior: Drop the unknown entry or mark it declined just because another event was processed.
claims.why_others_miss: A released terminal entry can produce perfectly consistent totals while losing the unresolved status this claim protects.
claims.does_not_cover: Its own approved or declined processor result is excluded. The conclusion does not freeze global counters or check their accuracy.
claims.risk: Drop the unknown entry or mark it declined just because another event was processed.

claims.title: Request outside work for the right hold
claims.scenario: Key 11 is authorized for 300¢. Cancelling it returns voiding while retaining the hold.
claims.must_happen: A voiding result must request the void for key 11. Dispatched and retried results must request authorization with the stored key and amount.
claims.wrong_behavior: Omit the required void request, as M7 does, or retry under a different authorization key, as M3 does.
claims.why_others_miss: A valid state that retains the hold can still omit the remote work. That is the gap exposed by P02.
claims.does_not_cover: The predicate branches on the supplied result. P01’s voided result with no effects passes it; retention rejects that premature release. Delivery is a separate concern.
claims.risk: Omit the required void request, as M7 does, or retry under a different authorization key, as M3 does.

claims.title: Keep a valid account valid after one event
claims.scenario: A valid account holds 100¢. Send it a request, timeout, restart or even a malformed event term.
claims.must_happen: Ledger.step must return a next state that still satisfies the entry, counter and capacity rules.
claims.wrong_behavior: Let an event-dispatch branch produce entries whose holding amount differs from the stored used amount.
claims.why_others_miss: Operation-specific checks do not alone describe the single dispatcher through which arbitrary event terms pass.
claims.does_not_cover: This is a state-validity promise. Exact results, required admission, retained identities and requested effects need their own claims.
claims.risk: Let an event-dispatch branch produce entries whose holding amount differs from the stored used amount.

claims.title: Keep the account valid through a finite event list
claims.scenario: Start with a valid account holding 100¢. Run dispatch, timeout and retry in order, followed by any further finite list of events.
claims.must_happen: Ledger.run must finish in a valid state for every proper finite event list.
claims.wrong_behavior: Fold the list using an outdated intermediate state so that the final counters no longer match its entries.
claims.why_others_miss: One-step preservation addresses individual transitions. This claim also covers how Ledger.run composes them.
claims.does_not_cover: The list must be proper and finite. The fold discards requested effects and does not establish delivery or wall-clock progress.
claims.risk: Fold the list using an outdated intermediate state so that the final counters no longer match its entries.

claims.title: Keep event histories valid from initialization
claims.scenario: Initialize a 100¢ account, then replay a finite list containing a request, dispatch and timeout.
claims.must_happen: The state produced by initialization followed by Ledger.run must satisfy validity for nonnegative integer limits.
claims.wrong_behavior: Combine initialization and replay incorrectly so the replayed 100¢ entry is paired with empty-account counters.
claims.why_others_miss: PO-C1 assumes a valid starting state. This claim connects the run directly to the state made by initialization.
claims.does_not_cover: A journal prefix is one such event list. The claim does not establish which records reached durable storage or execute their historical effects.
claims.risk: Combine initialization and replay incorrectly so the replayed 100¢ entry is paired with empty-account counters.

claims.title: Require an approval before marking a hold authorized
claims.scenario: Key 11 is sent for 300¢. A transport acknowledgment arrives without a processor approval.
claims.must_happen: A previously non-authorized entry may become authorized only on its own approved result, starting from sent or unknown.
claims.wrong_behavior: Mark key 11 authorized merely because delivery was acknowledged. M6 introduces this mistake.
claims.why_others_miss: Sent and authorized both consume 300¢ and one slot, so that unauthorized status change can pass accounting checks.
claims.does_not_cover: The helper checks entries present before the event. It does not by itself rule out a fabricated new authorized entry or establish a real processor’s honesty.
claims.risk: Mark key 11 authorized merely because delivery was acknowledged. M6 introduces this mistake.

claims.title: Keep a declined hold declined
claims.scenario: Key 11 is remembered as declined for 100¢. A delayed approved result or a repeated request arrives.
claims.must_happen: The same key and amount must still be recorded with declined status after the event.
claims.wrong_behavior: Revive the declined entry as authorized when the late approved result arrives.
claims.why_others_miss: Retaining a key and its amount does not preserve its terminal status. Correct counters can also accompany a wrongly revived entry.
claims.does_not_cover: This protects a local terminal entry over one step. Preventing a remote processor from creating an authorization is a separate fencing requirement.
claims.risk: Revive the declined entry as authorized when the late approved result arrives.

claims.title: Keep a cancelled hold voided
claims.scenario: Key 11 is remembered as voided for 100¢. A late result arrives after the hold has released its capacity.
claims.must_happen: The entry must remain voided with the same key and original amount after any next event.
claims.wrong_behavior: Change the voided entry back to sent or authorized in response to delayed traffic.
claims.why_others_miss: The identity claim preserves the entry’s key and amount but permits its status to change. This claim preserves the terminal status too.
claims.does_not_cover: Voided can follow a local cancellation before dispatch or a confirmed remote void. This local rule does not prove remote fencing.
claims.risk: Change the voided entry back to sent or authorized in response to delayed traffic.

claims.title: Remember every existing key and amount
claims.scenario: Key 11 holds 100¢ and key 22 holds 50¢. Process an event for key 11.
claims.must_happen: Both original keys must remain recorded with their original amounts in the next state.
claims.wrong_behavior: Remove key 22 or change its 50¢ amount while updating key 11.
claims.why_others_miss: Recomputing correct counters after deleting an entry can leave a valid account while erasing a remembered identity.
claims.does_not_cover: The conclusion allows status changes. P07 keeps key 1 and its amount but wrongly voids it, so exposure retention is needed as well.
claims.risk: Remove key 22 or change its 50¢ amount while updating key 11.

claims.title: Turn in-flight sends into uncertainty on restart
claims.scenario: Key 11 is sent for 300¢ when the process restarts.
claims.must_happen: Restart must leave no sent entries and preserve the used amount and hold count.
claims.wrong_behavior: Leave key 11 marked sent after restart, as M9 does, instead of acknowledging that its outcome is now uncertain.
claims.why_others_miss: The unchanged sent state is internally valid. A validity-only restart check therefore misses this status requirement.
claims.does_not_cover: This is the modeled restart transition. Finding and replaying the durable journal prefix belongs to recovery and runtime handling.
claims.risk: Leave key 11 marked sent after restart, as M9 does, instead of acknowledging that its outcome is now uncertain.

claims.title: Follow the reference behavior across a whole history
claims.scenario: Run a 100¢ hold through request, dispatch, approval, cancellation and confirmation, then process a late approval.
claims.must_happen: The final state must equal the independent expected run, preserve earlier identities and terminal entries, and have approvals explained along the reference history.
claims.wrong_behavior: Finish a history with a revived terminal hold or a final state that differs from the independently defined event sequence.
claims.why_others_miss: Validity across a history can still permit the wrong statuses or admission decisions. Reference agreement adds those behavioral requirements.
claims.does_not_cover: The claim covers proper finite event lists. Ledger.run returns state and discards results and effects, so effect execution remains outside this conclusion.
claims.risk: Finish a history with a revived terminal hold or a final state that differs from the independently defined event sequence.

claims.title: Keep confirmation’s counters consistent
claims.scenario: Key 11 is voiding for 100¢ and occupies one slot. Process a void confirmation.
claims.must_happen: The next state must satisfy validity, including agreement between holding entries and the stored amount and slot counters.
claims.wrong_behavior: Mark key 11 voided but leave its 100¢ counted as used, or subtract its slot twice.
claims.why_others_miss: Removing a pending-work record does not by itself check the ledger’s remaining amount and count.
claims.does_not_cover: The written law checks validity only. The event policy and composite confirmation claim describe which hold may release and how repeated confirmation behaves.
claims.risk: Mark key 11 voided but leave its 100¢ counted as used, or subtract its slot twice.

claims.title: Stop new attempts after the lifecycle is poisoned
claims.scenario: The attempt lifecycle has been marked poisoned. A new authorization attempt is requested for key 11.
claims.must_happen: Return the unchanged lifecycle state and no intents when asked to start another attempt.
claims.wrong_behavior: Spawn another authorization worker even though the lifecycle is already poisoned.
claims.why_others_miss: An empty operation slot and room under the attempt limit do not make a poisoned lifecycle eligible to start work.
claims.does_not_cover: The law describes the pure Attempts.step response to a start event. It does not establish how the runtime detects a failure or stops existing workers.
claims.risk: Spawn another authorization worker even though the lifecycle is already poisoned.

claims.title: Keep a delayed authorization behind the processor’s fence
claims.scenario: The modeled processor has a voided record for key 11. A delayed authorization for that key arrives with an approved outcome.
claims.must_happen: The environment must remain unchanged and return declined for that delayed authorization.
claims.wrong_behavior: Create a remotely live authorization for key 11 after its voided record has already fenced the key.
claims.why_others_miss: Ignoring a late reply in the local ledger does not prevent the processor from creating a remote authorization.
claims.does_not_cover: This proves a behavior of Environment’s model. A real adapter must honor the permanent-fencing contract, including delayed delivery.
claims.risk: Create a remotely live authorization for key 11 after its voided record has already fenced the key.

claims.title: Ignore events for an attempt that is no longer present
claims.scenario: Attempt 7 has left the attempt list. A late result, worker-down message or deadline still names it.
claims.must_happen: Result, down, deadline, shutdown-result and committed events for the absent ID must leave the state unchanged and emit no intents.
claims.wrong_behavior: Treat the late result for attempt 7 as a reason to persist or retire it again.
claims.why_others_miss: The active attempts can still have unique IDs and free slots while a stale event requests work for an absent ID.
claims.does_not_cover: Absence is the precondition. This claim does not describe when an active attempt is allowed to retire.
claims.risk: Treat the late result for attempt 7 as a reason to persist or retire it again.

claims.title: Allow one active attempt per operation and key
claims.scenario: An authorization attempt for key 11 is already active. Another start requests authorization for the same key.
claims.must_happen: Refuse the new start by returning the unchanged lifecycle state and no intents.
claims.wrong_behavior: Spawn a second authorization attempt for key 11 while the first still occupies that operation/key slot.
claims.why_others_miss: A global worker limit may still have room. The occupied-slot check prevents two attempts from competing for the same operation.
claims.does_not_cover: The slot is the pair of operation kind and key. An authorization and a lookup for the same key are different slots.
claims.risk: Spawn a second authorization attempt for key 11 while the first still occupies that operation/key slot.

claims.title: Keep issued holds counted until their own release evidence
claims.scenario: Key 11 is authorized for 100¢. Request cancellation before a terminal confirmation has arrived.
claims.must_happen: The same key and amount must remain in a holding status: sent, unknown, authorized or voiding.
claims.wrong_behavior: Release the 100¢ immediately after requesting a remote void, as M10 does, while the old authorization may still be live.
claims.why_others_miss: A voided entry with released counters can be internally valid. P01 also shows that changing the supplied result can let the empty effects list pass.
claims.does_not_cover: The condition excludes that key’s declined result and void confirmation. Other keys can change global totals; real processor truth and fencing remain external requirements.
claims.risk: Release the 100¢ immediately after requesting a remote void, as M10 does, while the old authorization may still be live.

claims.title: Replay committed work into the same combined state
claims.scenario: A committed cancellation leaves a 100¢ hold voiding and its remote void work still pending. Replay the same committed events.
claims.must_happen: The composite fold must reconstruct the identical modeled state, including pending obligations and their recorded metadata.
claims.wrong_behavior: Rebuild the ledger’s hold entries but lose the outstanding void obligation during replay.
claims.why_others_miss: Two recovered states can both be valid while recording different pending work. Replay equality requires the same state.
claims.does_not_cover: The theorem starts from a finite sequence of committed modeled transitions. It does not establish which writes a disk actually preserved.
claims.risk: Rebuild the ledger’s hold entries but lose the outstanding void obligation during replay.

claims.title: Keep one issued hold protected through a history
claims.scenario: A 100¢ authorization is sent. Timeout, retry and restart follow, with no decline or void confirmation for that key.
claims.must_happen: After the finite event history, the original key and amount must still be present in a protected holding status in a valid state.
claims.wrong_behavior: Release the old authorization’s 100¢ somewhere in the sequence despite receiving no terminal evidence for that key.
claims.why_others_miss: One retention step does not itself state the result of the whole fold. This theorem carries the protection through every event in the list.
claims.does_not_cover: The history excludes that key’s declined result and void confirmation. It establishes local retention, not a promise that the processor will eventually respond.
claims.risk: Release the old authorization’s 100¢ somewhere in the sequence despite receiving no terminal evidence for that key.

claims.title: Bound remote exposure using its authorization history
claims.scenario: An account allows 100¢ and one hold. A remote authorization for 100¢ can be traced to a valid local authorization request.
claims.must_happen: The total amount and count of remote live authorizations must stay within the account’s amount and hold limits.
claims.wrong_behavior: Count two independent remote authorizations against a single local 100¢ hold when retries were supposed to reuse one identity.
claims.why_others_miss: Local counters cannot reveal a processor that duplicates authorization identities. The theorem explicitly requires deduplication and a causal history for each remote authorization.
claims.does_not_cover: The bound depends on unique remote keys and histories with no terminal release evidence for authorizations still counted as live. Those processor premises need real-world support.
claims.risk: Count two independent remote authorizations against a single local 100¢ hold when retries were supposed to reuse one identity.

claims.title: Keep attempt IDs and slots distinct across a history
claims.scenario: Start an authorization attempt, receive its result, commit it, and then process a late worker-down event.
claims.must_happen: The typed finite history must preserve unique attempt IDs and operation/key slots, maintain ID bounds, and retire each ID at most once. A committing attempt ignores further completion events.
claims.wrong_behavior: Reuse an active attempt ID or emit a second retirement for the same ID later in the history.
claims.why_others_miss: Single-event refusal checks do not describe ID allocation and retirement across an entire lifecycle. This theorem also connects the typed steps to translated Attempts.step.
claims.does_not_cover: The history begins at the typed initial state. The theorem models events and intents; it does not schedule real workers.
claims.risk: Reuse an active attempt ID or emit a second retirement for the same ID later in the history.

claims.title: Start the ledger and pending work in agreement
claims.scenario: Initialize the combined state with a 100¢ amount limit and two hold slots.
claims.must_happen: The result must satisfy composite validity: a valid ledger, valid obligation records and the required correspondence between voiding keys and pending void work.
claims.wrong_behavior: Start with an outstanding void obligation for key 11 even though the ledger contains no such hold.
claims.why_others_miss: An empty ledger can be valid while unrelated pending-work records are wrong. Ledger initialization checks do not inspect that second part.
claims.does_not_cover: The theorem takes nonnegative integer limits. It covers modeled initialization, before any journal file is read.
claims.risk: Start with an outstanding void obligation for key 11 even though the ledger contains no such hold.

claims.title: Keep pending void work paired with the ledger
claims.scenario: A 100¢ hold is voiding and has one pending void obligation. Process another composite event.
claims.must_happen: The next state must preserve full composite validity, including valid obligation metadata and exactly one obligation for every voiding key.
claims.wrong_behavior: Leave the hold voiding but remove its obligation, so the ledger remembers a cancellation that the pending-work list has forgotten.
claims.why_others_miss: The ledger’s counters and entries can remain valid while its outstanding work falls out of agreement.
claims.does_not_cover: The claim checks the combined invariant. The oracle claim compares the complete result with independently specified behavior.
claims.risk: Leave the hold voiding but remove its obligation, so the ledger remembers a cancellation that the pending-work list has forgotten.

claims.title: Match the independent reference for a combined step
claims.scenario: Key 11 is authorized for 100¢. Apply a cancellation to both the composite implementation and its independent reference.
claims.must_happen: The complete step outputs must agree: next combined state, result and requested effects.
claims.wrong_behavior: Return a structurally valid combined state but the wrong result or different pending-void metadata from the independent reference.
claims.why_others_miss: Composite validity can allow several different states. Equality to the reference also specifies which transition occurred.
claims.does_not_cover: The comparison assumes a valid composite input. Agreement still needs review against the policy, since two implementations can share a misunderstanding.
claims.risk: Return a structurally valid combined state but the wrong result or different pending-void metadata from the independent reference.

claims.title: Keep the combined state consistent through a finite run
claims.scenario: Run a 100¢ hold through authorization, cancellation, restart and confirmation while tracking its pending void work.
claims.must_happen: The finite run must succeed, preserve full composite validity, correspond to committed modeled steps and agree with the independent composite run.
claims.wrong_behavior: Carry a stale obligation into the final state because the history fold missed the confirmation that removed it.
claims.why_others_miss: A correct single-step function still needs a correctly composed history fold. This claim connects both while retaining reference agreement.
claims.does_not_cover: The events form a finite list. Committed steps here describe the pure model, not evidence of physical journal synchronization.
claims.risk: Carry a stale obligation into the final state because the history fold missed the confirmation that removed it.

claims.title: Finish a pending void once
claims.scenario: Key 11 is voiding for 100¢ with a matching obligation. Process its trusted confirmation, then the same confirmation again.
claims.must_happen: The first confirmation must return voided with no effects and a valid combined state, removing the obligation. The repeat must return stale and leave that state unchanged.
claims.wrong_behavior: Remove the obligation on the first confirmation, then subtract another 100¢ or another slot when the confirmation is repeated.
claims.why_others_miss: A validity check does not alone specify the first and repeated results. This theorem fixes the complete repeated-confirmation behavior.
claims.does_not_cover: The starting composite state must be valid and the hold voiding. The runtime is responsible for admitting trusted confirmations.
claims.risk: Remove the obligation on the first confirmation, then subtract another 100¢ or another slot when the confirmation is repeated.

claims.title: Record the void work when cancellation begins
claims.scenario: Key 11 is authorized for 100¢ and has no pending void obligation. Request cancellation.
claims.must_happen: Return voiding, request the matching remote void, and append exactly one fresh obligation with zero attempts and an unattempted outcome.
claims.wrong_behavior: Request the remote cancellation but forget to record the outstanding work that recovery will need.
claims.why_others_miss: An effects check can see the correct void request while saying nothing about the companion pending-work records.
claims.does_not_cover: This theorem starts with a valid composite state and an authorized hold. A reserved-only cancellation follows the separate local-release path.
claims.risk: Request the remote cancellation but forget to record the outstanding work that recovery will need.

claims.title: Preserve combined validity across committed work
claims.scenario: A valid combined state contains a voiding 100¢ hold and its obligation. Follow a finite sequence of committed transitions.
claims.must_happen: The final committed state must still satisfy the complete ledger-and-obligation invariant.
claims.wrong_behavior: Commit a sequence whose final state has two void obligations for one hold or an obligation with invalid metadata.
claims.why_others_miss: Replay equality alone can reconstruct the same bad state. This theorem adds the invariant required of the committed result.
claims.does_not_cover: It assumes a valid starting state and the modeled committed relation. Disk durability and selection of the recovered prefix need separate evidence.
claims.risk: Commit a sequence whose final state has two void obligations for one hold or an obligation with invalid metadata.

claims.title: Keep the ledger and modeled processor in agreement
claims.scenario: A 100¢ hold is dispatched, delivered to the modeled processor, cancelled and confirmed. Track local state alongside issued requests and remote records.
claims.must_happen: Initialization, each modeled step and every finite run must preserve the combined exposure invariant. The registered void-before-issue result also keeps a delayed authorization fenced.
claims.wrong_behavior: Let a modeled delivery create a live remote authorization with no corresponding local held capacity.
claims.why_others_miss: The ledger and processor can each look internally consistent while disagreeing about which authorizations are live. The combined invariant checks their relationship.
claims.does_not_cover: The modeled environment follows explicit delivery and fencing rules. A real processor must supply evidence that it honors those rules.
claims.risk: Let a modeled delivery create a live remote authorization with no corresponding local held capacity.

claims.title: Read remote capacity bounds from the combined invariant
claims.scenario: A valid combined exposure state has a 100¢ amount limit, one slot and a remote live authorization for key 11.
claims.must_happen: The remote live amount must be at most 100¢ and the live authorization count at most one.
claims.wrong_behavior: Allow a combined state to pass its invariant while its remote records contain more live amount or authorizations than the local limits permit.
claims.why_others_miss: A collection of structural checks is useful only if it implies the intended numeric limits. This theorem makes that implication explicit.
claims.does_not_cover: The premise is full exposure validity. The separate exposure-bounds theorem instead takes deduplication and causal-history premises directly.
claims.risk: Allow a combined state to pass its invariant while its remote records contain more live amount or authorizations than the local limits permit.

claims.title: Request persistence once before retiring an attempt
claims.scenario: Attempt 7 produces a result and enters committing. Another completion arrives before a committed event retires it.
claims.must_happen: The finite typed history must request persistence at most once for each attempt ID. Retirement on a committed event must have an earlier persistence request for that ID.
claims.wrong_behavior: Emit two persistence requests for attempt 7, or retire it without any earlier persistence request in the modeled history.
claims.why_others_miss: Unique active IDs and at-most-once retirement do not establish the ordering or uniqueness of persistence requests.
claims.does_not_cover: These are persistence intents in the lifecycle model. The theorem does not establish that a journal write or fsync actually completed.
claims.risk: Emit two persistence requests for attempt 7, or retire it without any earlier persistence request in the modeled history.
